summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply of their own force and bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. A House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee report on the overseas territories in the 2007-08 session sets accountability and good-governance expectations covering Gibraltar, and the committee's 2008 enquiry recommended that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal in all overseas territories. That recommendation is not self-executing; Gibraltar legislates for itself.

Gender recognition is the principal gap. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor arrives on a document that no local route can alter and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

The Equal Opportunities Act 2006, in force from 1 March 2007, prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on the ground of "gender reassignment", defined as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. Coverage therefore turns on a physiological or comparable process rather than on identity or presentation, and a visitor who has not undergone such a process may fall outside the protected category.

The Crimes Act 2011 was amended in 2013, approved on 19 September, assented on 25 September and effective from 10 October 2013, to criminalise hatred and harassment on the ground of sexual orientation. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for "transgender identity". The Ministry for Justice and Equality said in July 2021 that it would urgently consider further legislation after abuse directed at gay people, and the ministry was examining a possible specific offence of denigrating a person on the ground of sexual orientation, following what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called "disgusting lurking homophobia" on social media during Pride month.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy. The sourced excerpt states the offence generally and does not specify whether it covers sexual orientation, transgender scope, or both.

Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014 and carry most rights of marriage, including adoption, as mandated by a 2013 court ruling. Marriage for same-sex couples was legalised by the Civil Marriage Amendment Act 2016, passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, given royal assent on 1 November and in force from 15 December 2016, with the first such marriage the following day. The bill followed a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians divided, and a government minister chaired an inter-ministerial committee that weighed the views submitted. A deputy registrar who opts out of solemnising is replaced by an alternative registrar. Because Gibraltar has no gender-recognition process, whether a trans visitor's relationship can be registered may depend on how local law reads the parties' birth-sex status.

The age of consent is 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender. The gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011 and effective from 23 November 2012, set that uniform age, after the Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that an age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional. A private member's bill to equalise the age of consent had been defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. Male same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 1993 under pressure from the European Court of Human Rights and the United Kingdom government.
tangentialFactors:
Abuse directed at gay people in 2021 drew a commitment from the Ministry for Justice and Equality to consider legislation urgently, and the Chief Minister attributed the pressure to abuse on social media during Pride month. The hostility documented in the sourced material is directed at gay men; no trans-specific incident is recorded.

The December 2015 consultation on the marriage bill left Gibraltarians polarised, with the main parties and the consultation process indicating support for the change. The registrar opt-out attaches an individual conscience provision to marriage solemnisation, though an alternative registrar is assigned.

Protection for trans people in Gibraltar has arrived through amendments to hate crime and hate speech legislation and through a general conversion therapy offence rather than through a dedicated gender recognition statute, which leaves the marker question untouched while the protections expand.

The Foreign Affairs Committee's recommendation that gender-status discrimination be outlawed across the overseas territories dates from 2008, and Gibraltar's own discrimination statute uses a narrower, process-based definition of gender reassignment.
localsOnly:
Adoption: the Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, legalising adoption by same-sex couples in substance, after a long-term lesbian couple were refused adoption for want of legal recognition of their relationship. The government amended the law through the 2014 civil partnership legislation, and the Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024, explicitly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

Assisted reproduction: in June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority amended its in vitro fertilisation policy to allow lesbian couples access to the technology. A February 2021 surrogacy law permits non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination.

Civil partnerships grant most rights of marriage, including adoption. Residents have no route to a corrected local gender marker, since no gender recognition process exists, and documents issued locally continue to follow birth-sex status.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the United Kingdom's equality legislation or service-provision codes have been extended to Gibraltar by Order in Council is not resolved in the sourced material; absent such an extension they do not apply here of their own force.

The 2006 Constitution does not mention sexual orientation, after 2002 proposals omitted it, so no constitutional equality guarantee on these grounds is recorded.

Commencement dates and any prosecutions or enforcement data for the July 2026 hate crime and hate speech amendment and the July 2026 conversion therapy offence are not sourced. The conversion therapy provision is stated generally in the sourced excerpt, which does not specify whether it covers sexual orientation alone, transgender scope, or both.

Sourced accounts differ on eligibility for surrogacy: one describes the February 2021 law as open to married couples or civil partners, another adds individuals. Whether the local definition of "gender reassignment", which turns on a physiological or comparable process, is applied to trans visitors in practice is not documented in the sourced material.
